items.actClause: AN ACT to amend the public housing law, in relation to preferences and priorities for prospective public housing and section 8 tenants in the city of New York
items.memo:
BILL NUMBER:S4558

TITLE OF BILL:

An act to amend the public housing law, in relation to preferences and
priorities for prospective public housing and section 8 tenants in the
city of New York

PURPOSE OR GENERAL IDEA OF BILL:

Requires the New York City Housing Authority, in reviewing applicants,
to grant homeless domestic violence victims the same preference as
granted the homeless

SUMMARY OF SPECIFIC PROVISIONS:

Section 1. Amends paragraph (e) of subdivision 3 of section 402-b of
the public housing law, as added by chapter 3 of the laws of 2010, to
provide that residency in a city owned, operated or contracted
domestic violence shelter shall be treated the same a residency in a
city owned, operated or contracted homeless shelter, for purposes of
calculating an applicant's priority status for public housing

Section 2. Effective immediately

JUSTIFICATION:

The New York City Housing Authority currently has a significant
backlog of qualified applicants for its available units, meaning that
individuals and families often wait years to obtain public housing.
Adding to this delay is the fact that preference categories have been
created to move specific categories of applicants with particularly
pressing housing needs to the top of the list. NYCHA has recently
reinstated a top N-0 priority for applicants who have spent more than
a year in a New York City homeless shelter.  Domestic violence
survivors are allowed to count time spent in a city-owned domestic
violence shelter toward the one-year requirement, but not time spent
in shelters operated by outside non-profits.  Because the city-owned
domestic violence shelter has a six month maximum length of stay, a
resident or family would have to transfer to a city homeless shelter
for six months instead of a privately-operated domestic violence
shelter in order to qualify for N-O status and maximize their chance
of obtaining public housing. No family should be forced to choose
between the security and vital services offered in a domestic violence
shelter and the chance to obtain permanent housing.

PRIOR LEGISLATIVE HISTORY:

New Legislation

FISCAL IMPLICATIONS:

None to the state.

EFFECTIVE DATE:

This act shall take effect immediately.
